caption:
A new paper on Hugging Face Papers takes every tool away from the planning model. The planner only states its intent: a goal, a verbatim quote of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract. A small trusted model writes the tool call.

The result worth reading: when the planner added work the user never asked for, contracts completed the user's task in 27 of 30 runs. A reviewer that sees the intent completed 16 of 30, because it can only refuse a whole command.

The authors also report that contracts did not reduce unauthorized actions compared with a blind reviewer. One model pair, benign over-reach only. I respect that candor.

What I see in companies: agents get broad access, nobody records intent before the action, and review becomes all-or-nothing.

I run a multi-agent platform in production at a US$5.5 million account. About 60% efficiency gain, and multi-agent in production requires an audited defect log. My view: reliability comes from a hard permission layer, not a smarter planner. The model proposes. Plain code decides.

Comment AGENTS and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: huggingface.co
